name: Horny goat weed (Epimedium)

card.summary: A Chinese medicinal herb sold as a libido and erection supplement; its flavonoid icariin inhibits PDE5 in the lab, but human trial evidence is minimal.
card.aka: Epimedium, yin yang huo, barrenwort, icariin
card.note: Evidence for sexual benefit comes mainly from animal and in vitro work; no published human trial on libido was found.

quick.overview:
Horny goat weed refers to plants of the genus Epimedium, used for centuries in traditional Chinese medicine as a kidney and yang tonic. The supplement form is typically E. grandiflorum or extracts standardized to icariin, sold for libido and erectile function.
Icariin is a weak PDE5 inhibitor in vitro, and animal studies report improved erectile function. Wikipedia states there is little clinical evidence to date, and a recent review says clinical efficacy still needs confirmation in randomized trials.
quick.mechanism: In animal and cell studies icariin has been reported to act through nitric oxide/cGMP signaling, Rho kinase inhibition and weak PDE5 inhibition, the same enzyme targeted by sildenafil and tadalafil, though at far lower potency.
quick.risks: Human safety data are limited. It is sold as a dietary supplement; a US homeopathic-labelled testosterone-support product listing it advises consulting a physician if pregnant or breastfeeding. Interaction data with PDE5 inhibitor drugs are not established.

lead: Horny goat weed is the common English name for plants of the genus Epimedium (family Berberidaceae), most of which are native to China.[1][2] The Chinese name yin yang huo is rendered roughly as lascivious goat herb.[1] Traditional Chinese medicine has used it as a tonic for kidney yang deficiency, including low libido and fatigue.[2][3]

People take it as a capsule, tablet, powder or tea, usually as an Epimedium or icariin extract, for libido, erectile function and general vitality.[16] In the looksmaxxing and bodybuilding world its place is mainly as a men's sexual-health and virility supplement, sometimes discussed alongside testosterone-focused routines, rather than as something that changes appearance directly.[18]

Its supposed aphrodisiac activity is attributed to icariin, a prenylated flavonoid described as a weak PDE5 inhibitor in vitro.[1] Wikipedia states clinical effects are unknown and there is little clinical evidence to date.[1] Reviews of icariin describe erectogenic effects in animal models and say clinical confirmation in high-quality trials is still needed.[4][5]

chain: Icariin acts on nitric oxide and PDE5 pathways in lab models
Aims at better erectile function and drive, which some users link to feeling and presenting more vital
angle.text: Users take it for libido and erectile support, and some bodybuilding forum members add it to routines at the end of a gear cycle when they feel flat. Its link to appearance runs through sexual confidence and training drive rather than any direct cosmetic action.

infobox: Dietary supplement (US); not reviewed by the FDA for effectiveness [17]

paras: Traditional Chinese medicine uses the aerial parts for kidney-tonifying and yang-strengthening purposes, and the genus is documented for sexual dysfunction, osteoporosis and a range of other traditional indications.[3] A 2025 review of phytoestrogens in osteoporosis also lists Epimedium among plants examined for bone health.[12]

Western supplements sell Epimedium or icariin extracts for libido, erectile function and vitality, in tablets, capsules, powders and teas.[2][16] WebMD lists uses such as erectile dysfunction, osteoporosis, increasing sex drive in men and improving mental and physical performance, and describes the benefits for these as not well defined.[17] A 2014 paper reviewed sexual-enhancement products sold online containing yohimbine, maca, horny goat weed and Ginkgo biloba.[6]

Carl Linnaeus named the genus Epimedium in 1753, based on the European species E. alpinum; the name derives from a Greek plant name, epimedion, mentioned by Pliny, whose original meaning is unclear.[1] Wikipedia lists common names including barrenwort, bishop's hat and fairy wings.[1]

The English name 'horny goat weed' is said to come from a story in which a goat herder noticed increased sexual activity in his flock after they ate the plant, and barrenwort from a historical belief that it could cause infertility in women.[2] The Chinese name is translated as lascivious goat herb.[1]

Icariin is a prenylated flavonol glycoside, the 8-prenyl derivative of kaempferol 3,7-O-diglucoside, isolated from several Epimedium species also known as Herba epimedii.[15] The genus contains more than 260 compounds, mostly prenylflavonoids.[3] Other compounds such as epimedin C and icariside II appear in the plant and are studied separately.[1] Wikipedia names E. grandiflorum as the species used in dietary supplements.[1]

In vitro, icariin is a weak PDE5 inhibitor; Wikipedia notes that sildenafil, vardenafil and tadalafil are stronger, and Healthline reports a 2008 test-tube study in which sildenafil was about 80 times more potent.[1][16] Reviews describe actions on nitric oxide/cGMP signalling and Rho kinase in animal models, as well as neuroprotective, bone, anti-inflammatory and anticancer effects in laboratory models.[4][5][9][11]

The relative PDE5 potency of icariin is much lower than that of approved drugs.[1] WebMD says flavonoids and icariin may relax blood vessels and may influence how the body responds to testosterone and estrogen, possibly reducing bone loss.[17]

No dedicated randomized trial of horny goat weed or icariin for libido or erectile function has been found. Wikipedia states there is little clinical evidence to date.[1] Healthline describes research on human erectile tissue as limited and the overall picture as mixed.[16]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists small human studies of icariin for other purposes, including a pharmacokinetic study in healthy volunteers and a study in bipolar disorder with substance use.[7][14] A placebo-controlled crossover trial tested reishi, nettle and Epimedium for Gulf War illness, not for sexual function.[13]

A 2010 study in rats with cavernous nerve injury and in cultured pelvic ganglia reported erectogenic and neurotrophic effects of icariin.[8] A 2026 review of icariin in erectile dysfunction summarised mechanisms in animal models and concluded clinical efficacy needs confirmation in high-quality randomized trials.[4]

Systematic human safety data are limited. Memorial Sloan Kettering, as relayed by Healthline, lists possible effects such as sweating or flushing, rapid heartbeat, increased energy and mood changes, and Healthline advises caution for people with heart disease, high blood pressure or a history of hormone-sensitive cancer.[16] WebMD lists dry mouth, nausea, upset stomach and vertigo as common effects, severe allergic reactions as possible, and says safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding is unknown.[17]

WebMD reports possible interactions with nitrates, hormone therapy, birth control, and medicines for erectile dysfunction or pulmonary arterial hypertension, and notes that research on drug interactions is incomplete.[17] It also says some sexual-enhancement supplements have been found to contain undisclosed prescription drugs.[17] A US product label combining horny goat weed with other herbs advises consulting a health professional if pregnant or breastfeeding.[10]

sections.h: Use in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities
paras: On T Nation, horny goat weed turns up in supplement-store anecdotes, where an older couple asked a clerk for maca or horny goat weed to keep up their love life.[20] Forum members describe trying it: one says it did not make him last longer, and another writes that he took it after hearing about it from a YouTube comedy duo when feeling 'soft' at the end of a steroid cycle.[19][18]
Other threads treat it as a staple of the supplement shelf, with a long-running joke that someone will always recommend it when a thread goes quiet.[21]

Related herbal and supplement approaches include maca, tribulus, yohimbine and ginkgo, which are sold in the same sexual-enhancement categories.[6] Prescription PDE5 inhibitors such as sildenafil and tadalafil are the drugs whose target enzyme icariin acts on at lower potency.[1]

lore.intro: In bodybuilding and sexual-health forums horny goat weed is discussed as a cheap herbal libido and erectile aid, and as a supplement some members add when feeling flat at the end of a gear cycle.[18][21]

claims.claim: Horny goat weed boosts libido and erections like a mild Viagra.
claims.believers: Users and supplement sellers say icariin works on the same enzyme as sildenafil; a clerk anecdote shows customers asking for it by name.[20]
claims.experts: Icariin is a weak PDE5 inhibitor in vitro and animal studies report improved erectile function, but no published randomized trial has tested it for libido or erection in men.[1][4][8]

claims.claim: It helps a man 'feel less soft' after a steroid cycle.
claims.believers: One poster took it at the end of a cycle after hearing about it from a YouTube pair and felt he was getting soft.[18]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined Epimedium in the setting of anabolic steroid use.

claims.claim: It is a safe natural alternative to prescription ED drugs.
claims.believers: Supplement sellers describe it as a traditional herb.[2]
claims.experts: The FDA has not reviewed it for safety or effectiveness, possible interactions with nitrates and ED drugs are listed, and some sexual-enhancement supplements contain undisclosed drugs.[17]

claims.claim: It supports bone and general vitality as a kidney tonic.
claims.believers: Traditional Chinese medicine practitioners use it for kidney yang deficiency, osteoporosis and fatigue.[3]
claims.experts: Reviews describe bone and neuroprotective effects in laboratory models and early clinical work, and call for confirmation in controlled trials.[11][12]
